h1: Finding a mentor in the brewing industry
title: Finding a Mentor in Brewing | Craft Beer School
desc: How to find a mentor in the brewing industry: where to look, what to ask for, how to approach and how to keep the relationship useful.
teaser: A good mentor shortens years of trial and error. Most are found by showing up and asking a specific question.
standfirst: Brewing is a small trade where the people who know the most are often busy. They still answer well-made questions. Here is where to find a mentor and how to ask.
sections: What a mentor does and does not do

A mentor is someone with more experience who gives you honest advice over time. In brewing that often means a head brewer, a founder or an instructor who has already made the mistakes you are about to make. They tell you which job to take, which mistake to avoid and who to meet. They do not give you a job, do your homework or fix your brewing for you. Think of a mentor as a conversation every month or two, not a daily teacher. A twenty minute call that you prepared for beats a long chat that wanders.

You may need more than one. A head brewer helps with technical work. A founder helps with the business. Someone who changed careers helps with the leap. Pick the question you most need answered and look for the person who has answered it.

• Taprooms and brewpubs. Visit on a quiet afternoon, buy a beer and ask the brewer one question about the beer in your glass. Do not ask for a job in the same visit.
  • Homebrew clubs and meetups. The people who judge competitions and teach classes are often professionals.
  • Beer festivals and trade events. Brewers stand behind their tables and talk. Go early before the crowd.
  • Courses and certifications. Instructors are working practitioners. Our guides on brewing certifications and the Cicerone programme show the routes.
  • Online. Professional networks and brewing forums. A thoughtful comment on someone's post gets noticed more than a cold message.

A busy brewer will not teach you what a book can. Read the basics first, brew a few batches and note what went wrong. Then ask about a specific problem. "How do I become a brewer?" is too big. "My ale finishes at 1.018 when the recipe says 1.012; I mash at 68 °C and pitch one packet of dry yeast. What would you check first?" gets an answer.

Specific questions show you have done the work. They also let a busy person answer in two minutes. Our guide on how to become a brewer in India gives the wider route to prepare for.
How to make the first approach

Write a short message. Say who you are, name one thing you admire about their work, ask one question and offer a time that suits them. Fifteen minutes by phone or a coffee near their work is a fair request. Do not send a long life story or attach a CV unless asked.

If they do not reply, wait two weeks and send one polite follow-up. After that, move on. Brewers are busy and silence is rarely personal.

A mentor gains from the relationship too. Offer to help on a brew day by carrying sacks and cleaning kit. Volunteering for a few hours teaches more than a month of reading. It also shows you can work. You can share what you learn about a new topic, such as a testing method or a software tool. Bring a beer you made and ask for honest feedback.

Never ask a mentor for an introduction in the first meeting. Wait until they know you.

After each conversation, send a two line thank-you and note what you will try. A month later, tell them what happened. That small loop is what makes someone want to keep helping. Ask for advice, then act on at least some of it. A mentor who sees you ignoring every suggestion will stop offering.

Respect their time. Meet rarely, come prepared and end on time. If the relationship changes, thank them and keep in touch. Our guide on learning to brew professionally while keeping your day job offers ways to fit this around work.

This week, write down the single biggest question you have about brewing. Find one person who could answer it: a brewer whose beer you like, an instructor or a club member. Send a short message with that question. A structured course such as Brewing Fundamentals also gives you a first set of working brewers to learn from and a shared vocabulary for the questions.
faqs: Can I ask a head brewer to be my mentor straight away?
It is better to start with one specific question and build the relationship. Most mentors emerge from repeated, useful conversations rather than a formal request.
Where do I find mentors if I do not live near a brewery?
Online brewing forums, professional networks, live online courses and virtual homebrew clubs. A thoughtful comment or question gets noticed more than a cold message.
Not usually. Mentoring is a favour built on goodwill. Offer help, thanks and feedback. Paid coaching or consulting is a different arrangement.
What if a mentor does not reply?
Wait two weeks, send one polite follow-up and then move on. Busy brewers miss messages. It is rarely personal.
